title: Telerehabilitation with or Without Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation in Older Stroke Survivors with Cognitive Impairment: A Three-Arm Randomised Trial
content: Background/Objectives: Evidence on telerehabilitation combined with transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) in older stroke survivors with cognitive impairment remains limited. This study compared Brunnstrom-based telerehabilitation (TRB), TRB plus tDCS, and a conventional physiotherapy intervention (CON). Methods: In this single-centre, assessor-blinded randomised trial, 87 participants were allocated equally to three eight-week programmes. Pain, motor recovery, balance, mobility and cognition were assessed at baseline and weeks 4 and 8. Repeated-measures analyses included 83 participants and adjusted for education, hypertension and diabetes. Results: Group-by-time effects were significant for Timed Up and Go (TUG; p < 0.001), Brunnstrom hand stage (p = 0.008) and lower-limb stage (p = 0.027). Only the TUG effect remained significant after accounting for the nine outcomes assessed. TUG improvement was greater with TRB plus tDCS than with TRB by 2.74 seconds (95% CI 1.32-4.17) and CON by 2.51 seconds (1.19-3.83). At week 8, hand-stage scores favoured the combined intervention over both comparators. Pain scores were lower than with TRB at weeks 4 and 8, but pain trajectories did not differ significantly. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) group-by-time effect was not significant (p = 0.880). Conclusions: Adding tDCS to telerehabilitation produced greater improvements in TUG performance than telerehabilitation alone or the conventional physiotherapy intervention over eight weeks. This mobility benefit remained statistically significant after accounting for the nine outcomes assessed. Telerehabilitation alone and conventional physiotherapy showed improvements in hand recovery, mobility and cognitive scores, without significant differences in their changes. No additional cognitive benefit from tDCS was demonstrated.
